title: Renal Cell Carcinoma
subject: Pathology
summary: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the commonest primary kidney cancer, arising from proximal tubular cells. It presents with haematuria, flank mass, or paraneoplastic syndromes and is staged by the TNM system.

sections.p: RCC is a malignant tumour of the renal tubular epithelium, most often clear‑cell type. Diagnosis requires imaging and histology.

t.b: Is there a solid renal mass? – A hyperechoic, heterogeneous mass suggests RCC; if unavailable, proceed to CT when possible.
What is the size, extent, and vascular involvement? – Shows enhancing mass, renal vein/IVC invasion; essential for staging.
Does histology confirm RCC subtype? – Provides definitive diagnosis when imaging is equivocal; not needed if classic imaging.

sections.p: Staging follows the AJCC TNM system; stage correlates with prognosis and guides surgery.
b: T3: renal vein/IVC or perinephric fat invasion

sections.p: Most RCCs are sporadic; several risk factors are common in low‑resource settings.
b: Acquired cystic kidney disease in dialysis

sections.p: Classic triad is rare; patients often have subtle or incidental findings.
b: Visible haematuria or painless gross blood in urine

sections.p: Imaging is the cornerstone; labs help identify paraneoplastic effects.
b: Serum calcium – hypercalcaemia in 10% of cases

t.b: Is there lung metastasis? – Detects pulmonary nodules; if unavailable, rely on clinical suspicion.
What is soft‑tissue detail and vascular invasion? – Useful for surgical planning.

sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent referral or indicate poor prognosis.
Curative intent is surgery; systemic therapy is for advanced disease.
b: Radical nephrectomy – gold standard for localized RCC
Partial nephrectomy – for small (<7 cm) tumours when renal function must be preserved
Targeted therapy (VEGF‑TKI e.g., sunitinib) – for metastatic disease; avoid if severe liver dysfunction
Immunotherapy (PD‑1 inhibitor) – alternative when TKIs contraindicated
Control hypertension, hypercalcaemia, and polycythemia symptomatically

sections.p: Long‑term surveillance detects recurrence; lifestyle modification reduces risk.
b: CT abdomen every 6‑12 months for 3 years, then annually
Screen high‑risk VHL patients with annual MRI

sections.p: Conditions that mimic RCC clinically or radiologically.
b: Angiomyolipoma – fat‑rich, benign, shows macroscopic fat on CT
Oncocytoma – central scar on imaging, benign
Renal abscess – fever, flank pain, may have fluid collection

sections.p: Pitfalls in interpretation that may delay correct diagnosis.
b: Small RCC may appear cystic on ultrasound, mistaken for benign cyst
Normal calcium does not exclude paraneoplastic syndrome
Negative biopsy can occur if sampling necrotic centre

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe flank pain with hypotension (possible tumour rupture)
Rapidly rising blood pressure or hypercalcaemia causing neurologic symptoms
New neurological deficits suggesting brain metastasis

faq.q: Why is smoking such a strong risk factor?
faq.a: Carcinogens in tobacco induce DNA damage in tubular cells, doubling RCC risk.

faq.q: Can RCC be cured without surgery?
faq.a: Only when disease is metastatic and limited; otherwise surgery offers the only curative chance.

faq.q: What causes the polycythemia in RCC?
faq.a: Tumour cells secrete erythropoietin, stimulating red‑cell production.

exam: A 58‑year‑old smoker presents with painless haematuria – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Order contrast CT abdomen to characterise a possible RCC; ultrasound alone may miss small lesions.
How does the presence of a renal vein thrombus change management? — Requires radical nephrectomy with thrombectomy; partial nephrectomy is insufficient.
Differentiate RCC from angiomyolipoma on imaging – what key feature helps? — Presence of macroscopic fat on CT indicates angiomyolipoma, absent in RCC.
A patient with RCC has a serum calcium of 12 mg/dL – what does this imply and how should you act? — Suggests paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia; treat with hydration, bisphosphonates, and address tumour.
Why is partial nephrectomy preferred for a 5 cm peripheral tumour in a patient with chronic kidney disease? — Preserves renal function while achieving oncologic control.
Explain why VEGF‑TKI therapy is avoided in a patient with severe liver failure. — These drugs are metabolised hepatically and can cause liver toxicity, worsening failure.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate referral to a surgical team? — Rapidly enlarging flank mass with signs of venous obstruction (e.g., leg swelling).
In a low‑resource setting without CT, how would you proceed if ultrasound shows a solid renal mass? — Arrange referral for CT if possible; if not, consider biopsy to confirm diagnosis before surgery.
